How to prompt Llama 3
The base models have no prompt format. Like other base models, they can be used to continue an input sequence with a plausible continuation or for zero-shot/few-shot inference. They are also a great foundation for fine-tuning your own use cases. The Instruct versions use the following conversation structure:
<|begin_of_text|><|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
{{ system_prompt }}<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
{{ user_msg_1 }}<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
{{ model_answer_1 }}<|eot_id|>
This format has to be exactly reproduced for effective use. We’ll later show how easy it is to reproduce the instruct prompt with the chat template available in transformers. 
Demo
You can chat with the Llama 3 70B instruct on Hugging Chat! Check out the link here: https://huggingface.co/chat/models/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-instruct
Using 🤗 Transformers
With Transformers release 4.40, you can use Llama 3 and leverage all the tools within the Hugging Face ecosystem, such as:
- training and inference scripts and examples
- safe file format (safetensors)
- integrations with tools such as bitsandbytes (4-bit quantization), PEFT (parameter efficient fine-tuning), and Flash Attention 2
- utilities and helpers to run generation with the model
- mechanisms to export the models to deploy
In addition, Llama 3 models are compatible with torch.compile() with CUDA graphs, giving them a ~4x speedup at inference time!
To use Llama 3 models with transformers, make sure to install a recent version of transformers:
pip install --upgrade transformers
The following snippet shows how to use Llama-3-8b-instruct with transformers. It requires about 16 GB of RAM, which includes consumer GPUs such as 3090 or 4090.
from transformers import pipeline
import torch
model_id = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct"
pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model=model_id,
    model_kwargs={"torch_dtype": torch.bfloat16},
    device="cuda",
)
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a pirate chatbot who always responds in pirate speak!"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"},
]
terminators = [
    pipe.tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    pipe.tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("<|eot_id|>")
]
outputs = pipe(
    messages,
    max_new_tokens=256,
    eos_token_id=terminators,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.6,
    top_p=0.9,
)
assistant_response = outputs[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"]
print(assistant_response)
Arrrr, me hearty! Me name be Captain Chat, the scurviest pirate chatbot to ever sail the Seven Seas! Me be here to swab the decks o' yer mind with me trusty responses, savvy? Gemini 1.5: Unlocking multimodal understanding across millions of tokens of context
Abstract
In this report, we introduce the Gemini 1.5 family of models, representing the next generation of highly compute-efficient multimodal models capable of recalling and reasoning over fine-grained information from millions of tokens of context, including multiple long documents and hours of video and audio. The family includes two new models: (1) an updated Gemini 1.5 Pro, which exceeds the February version on the great majority of capabilities and benchmarks; (2) Gemini 1.5 Flash, a more lightweight variant designed for efficiency with minimal regression in quality. Gemini 1.5 models achieve near-perfect recall on long-context retrieval tasks across modalities, improve the state-of-the-art in long-document QA, long-video QA and long-context ASR, and match or surpass Gemini 1.0 Ultra’s state-of-the-art performance across a broad set of benchmarks. Studying the limits of Gemini 1.5’s long-context ability, we find continued improvement in next-token prediction and near-perfect retrieval (>99%) up to at least 10M tokens, a generational leap over existing models such as Claude 3.0 (200k) and GPT-4 Turbo (128k). Finally, we highlight real-world use cases, such as Gemini 1.5 collaborating with professionals on completing their tasks achieving 26 to 75% time savings across 10 different job categories, as well as surprising new capabilities of large language models at the frontier; when given a grammar manual for Kalamang, a language with fewer than 200 speakers worldwide, the model learns to translate English to Kalamang at a similar level to a person who learned from the same content.
1 Introduction
We present our latest multimodal models from the Gemini line: Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash. They are members of Gemini 1.5, a new family of highly-capable multimodal models which incorporates our latest innovations in sparse and dense scaling as well as major advances in training, distillation and serving infrastructure that allow it to push the boundary of efficiency, reasoning, planning, multi-linguality, function calling and long-context performance. Gemini 1.5 models are built to handle extremely long contexts; they have the ability to recall and reason over fine-grained information from up to at least 10M tokens. This scale is unprecedented among contemporary large language models (LLMs), and enables the processing of long-form mixed-modality inputs including entire collections of documents, multiple hours of video, and almost five days long of audio.
The Gemini 1.5 Pro presented in this report is an update over the previous Gemini 1.5 Pro February version and it outperforms it predecessor on most capabilities and benchmarks. All in all, the Gemini 1.5 series represents a generational leap in model performance and training efficiency. Gemini 1.5 Pro surpasses Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.0 Ultra on a wide array of benchmarks while requiring significantly less compute to train. Similarly, Gemini 1.5 Flash performs uniformly better compared to 1.0 Pro and even performs at a similar level to 1.0 Ultra on several benchmarks.
The ability to model data of increasingly longer contexts has tracked the development of more general and capable language models, from the now toy 2-gram language model proposed by Shannon 1948, to the modern n-gram models of the 1990s & 2000s typically constrained to 5 tokens of context (Brants et al. 2007; Chen and Goodman 1999; Kneser and Ney 1995; Jelinek 1998), to recurrent neural networks language models from the 2010s which could effectively condition on hundreds of tokens (Mikolov et al. 2010; Jozefowicz et al. 2016), to the modern Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) which can condition on hundreds of thousands of tokens (Anthropic 2023a). Gemini 1.5 Pro continues this trend by extending language model context lengths by over an order of magnitude. Scaling to millions of tokens, we find a continued improvement in predictive performance (Section 5.2.1.1), near perfect recall (99%) on synthetic retrieval tasks (Figure 1 and Section 5.2.1.2), and a host of surprising new capabilities like in-context learning from entire long documents and multimodal content (Section 5.2.2).
To measure the effectiveness of our models’ multimodal long-context capabilities, we conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world tasks. In synthetic “needle-in-a-haystack” tasks inspired by Kamradt 2023 that probe how reliably the model can recall information amidst distractor context, we find that both Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash achieve near-perfect (99%) “needle” recall up to multiple millions of tokens of “haystack” in all modalities, i.e., text, video and audio. As part of our experimental setup, we also assessed the performance of Gemini 1.5 Pro when extending the context to 10M tokens across all three modalities. We found that the recall performance was maintained even with this significant increase in context size.

| 2023-08-31 (arXiv) / 2024-01-16 (OpenReview) | YaRN (RoPE extension method; not a model release, but key enabler) | Extends beyond pretraining length via efficient fine-tuning; mentions NTK-aware / Dynamic NTK variants used in models | YaRN abstract + intro describe “extend the context window… requiring 10x less tokens…” and discuss “NTK-aware” interpolation and use in open models (e.g., Code Llama). [https://arxiv.org/html/2309.00071] |
| 2023-11-06 | OpenAI GPT‑4 Turbo (preview) | 128K tokens | “GPT‑4 Turbo… supports a 128K context window… It has a 128k context window…” [https://openai.com/index/new-models-and-developer-products-announced-at-devday/] |
| 2024-04-18 | Meta Llama 3 (via HF launch post) | 8K tokens | “All the variants… have a context length of 8K tokens.” [https://huggingface.co/blog/llama3] |
| 2024-04-09 (arXiv) | RULER benchmark (evaluation; not a model release) | Evaluates models up to 128k; finds effective context often much smaller than claimed | “Despite achieving nearly perfect accuracy in… NIAH… almost all models exhibit large performance drops as the context length increases… While these models all claim context sizes of 32K tokens or greater, only half… can maintain satisfactory performance at… 32K.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06654] |
| 2024-03 (report; versioned updates described inside) | Gemini 1.5 (family) | Reports near-perfect retrieval up to millions of tokens; tested up to at least 10M tokens | “capable of recalling and reasoning… from millions of tokens… continued improvement… >99% up to at least 10M tokens.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2403.05530] |
| 2026-06-22 (docs page date shown in snippet) | Gemini API long context | 1,000,000-token context window (product docs) | The Gemini API “Long context” documentation snippet explicitly says “(1 million context window).” [https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context] |

### Explicit “what I did not find” (timeline gaps)
- **GPT‑3 2048 tokens (authoritative citation):** I accessed the GPT‑3 paper HTML, but the tool output was truncated and I did **not** locate the specific “2048 token” context length line within the captured text. [https://arxiv.org/html/2005.14165]
- **GPT‑2 1024 tokens (authoritative primary PDF):** I attempted to read the OpenAI GPT‑2 PDF, but the tool could not extract readable text from that PDF. [https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf]
- **Llama 2 4096 tokens (official primary source):** I did not retrieve a Meta primary source stating 4096; search results surfaced Meta’s Llama 2 publication page, but I did not open a page that explicitly states the context length in readable text within this run. [https://ai.meta.com/research/publications/llama-2-open-foundation-and-fine-tuned-chat-models/] *(not read/extracted here)*
- **Llama 3 “16k” variants:** I did not find an official Meta source in this run; I only captured the HF launch post asserting 8K. [https://huggingface.co/blog/llama3]
- **ALiBi primary paper:** web search for ALiBi timed out in this environment, so I did not capture a primary ALiBi citation. *(gap: no source captured)*
- **NTK-aware RoPE scaling primary citation:** I captured YaRN which discusses NTK-aware and related methods, but I did not capture the original NTK-aware preprint itself (only YaRN’s discussion of it). [https://arxiv.org/html/2309.00071]

---

## Part 2 — Limits that remain even with very large context windows (128k–1M+)

### A) Compute, memory & latency limits
- **Attention compute/memory grows rapidly with sequence length in vanilla Transformers.** “Transformers… require memory and compute that increases quadratically in sequence length.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172]
- **Even “exact attention” needs algorithmic/IO improvements to be practical at long lengths.** FlashAttention frames the core problem: “time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length,” and proposes IO-aware tiling to reduce memory traffic. [https://arxiv.org/html/2205.14135]
- **In practice, serving constraints persist (KV-cache, throughput) even when a model *accepts* long inputs.** I did **not** retrieve a primary source in this run quantifying KV-cache scaling; only a secondary/tertiary arXiv review snippet appeared in search results (not opened). Therefore, KV-cache scaling is a **gap** in sourced findings for this response. *(gap; no captured source)*

### B) Attention/architecture limits (positional encodings, extrapolation)
- **Many models don’t “generalize past the sequence length they were trained on” without special methods.** YaRN states: “these models fail to generalize past the sequence length they were trained on.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2309.00071]
- **Extending context often requires techniques like RoPE interpolation/scaling + (light) fine-tuning.** YaRN: “extend the context window… requiring 10x less tokens…” and claims LLaMA models can “utilize and extrapolate to context lengths much longer than their original pre-training would allow.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2309.00071]

### C) Effective context use (retrieval, “lost in the middle,” and real vs claimed context)
- **“Lost in the middle” effect:** performance is often best when relevant info is near the beginning/end, and worse when it’s in the middle. The paper reports a “U-shaped performance curve… highest when relevant information occurs at the very beginning… or end… and… degrades… in the middle of long contexts.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172]
- **Long context is a trade-off, not a free win.** The same work concludes longer contexts can reduce accuracy because there’s more to reason over: “prompting… with longer input contexts is a trade-off… increases the amount of content… potentially decreasing accuracy.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172]
- **Benchmarks show “effective” context can be far smaller than advertised.** RULER finds that despite perfect “needle” retrieval, “almost all models exhibit large performance drops as the context length increases,” and “only half… can maintain satisfactory performance at… 32K” despite claiming ≥32K. [https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06654]

### D) Training/data constraints
- **Long-context capability is tied to training and evaluation regime.** YaRN emphasizes the *training-process-determined* “maximal length of the sequences… has been one of the major limits,” motivating methods to extend via fine-tuning. [https://arxiv.org/html/2309.00071]
- **Even when a model is engineered for very long context, evaluation stresses “retrieval vs reasoning over long spans.”** Gemini 1.5 reports “near-perfect recall” on synthetic retrieval tasks at very long lengths, but that doesn’t by itself guarantee robust long-range reasoning across arbitrary tasks; this distinction is central to why RULER expands beyond “needle” tests. [https://arxiv.org/html/2403.05530], [https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06654]

### E) Safety & security limits (prompt injection, instruction hierarchy)
- **Prompt injection remains a recognized vulnerability class for LLM apps, and larger contexts increase the space for hidden/malicious instructions.** OWASP describes prompt injection as an attack that “manipulates the model’s behavior by crafting malicious or misleading prompts—often bypassing safety filters…” [https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/PromptInjection]
- **I did not find a sourced, quantitative claim tying *longer* windows specifically to higher injection success rates in this run.** OWASP describes the attack generally, but not a window-length scaling law. *(gap; no captured source)*

---

## Practical guidance checklist for using long context (grounded in the findings above)

- **Don’t assume “fits” means “used”:** test sensitivity to *position* of key facts (beginning/middle/end), because “lost in the middle” is common. [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172]
- **Prefer structure over raw dump:** organize content (headings, IDs, key-value blocks, citations) to reduce reasoning burden; longer contexts can be a trade-off that “potentially decreas[es] accuracy.” [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172]
- **Benchmark your task, not just needle retrieval:** RULER shows models can ace NIAH but fail at harder long-context behaviors as length grows. [https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06654]
- **Expect cost/latency to rise with length:** vanilla attention has quadratic scaling; rely on optimized kernels/implementations where possible (e.g., FlashAttention-style IO-aware exact attention) but still plan for higher runtime. [https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172], [https://arxiv.org/html/2205.14135]
- **Harden against prompt injection:** treat all retrieved/embedded/user-provided text as untrusted, because injection attacks can “manipulate the model’s behavior.” [https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/PromptInjection]

### Anthropic Claude: expanded to 100k tokens (May 11, 2023)
- Anthropic announcement: “**We’ve expanded Claude’s context window from 9K to 100K tokens** …”  
  Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/100k-context-windows

---

### Anthropic Claude 3 family (announced Mar 4, 2024): 200k tokens (with note about >1M capability)
- Anthropic announcement: “**The Claude 3 family of models will initially offer a 200K context window upon launch. However, all three models are capable of accepting inputs exceeding 1 million tokens** …”  
  Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-family

---

### Google Gemini 1.5 Pro (announced Feb 15, 2024): 128k standard; up to 1,000,000 tokens (preview)
- Google blog: “**Gemini 1.5 Pro comes with a standard 128,000 token context window… can try it with a context window of up to 1 million tokens** …”  
  Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/google-gemini-next-generation-model-february-2024/

---

## 2) Technical constraints that still apply at long context (with sources)

### A) Compute/memory scaling with long context (attention + quadratic costs)
- “Lost in the Middle” notes standard Transformers “**require memory and compute that increases quadratically in sequence length**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172 (Section 1 Introduction)

**What I did not find:** I did not successfully extract a direct quote from “Attention Is All You Need” explicitly stating O(n²) self-attention complexity; I relied on the long-context evaluation paper above for the quadratic scaling statement.

---

### B) KV cache memory scales with context length (linear growth; becomes dominant)
- KVQuant paper: “**with these large context windows KV cache activations surface as the dominant contributor to memory consumption during inference**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.18079 (Abstract)
- Same paper explains KV cache size growth: “**the KV cache size … grows linearly with both batch size and sequence length**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.18079 (Section 2.2)

Implication supported by source: even if attention compute is optimized, **serving** long context can hit a hard wall on GPU memory due to KV cache.

---

### C) Latency and cost pressures at very long context
- Google explicitly ties long context rollout to systems constraints: “**we’re actively working on optimizations to improve latency, reduce computational requirements and enhance the user experience**.”  
  Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/google-gemini-next-generation-model-february-2024/

**What I did not find:** I did not find a primary-source statement quantifying $/request or latency scaling as a function of context length for a specific model (beyond the general statement above).

---

### D) Performance degradation in long contexts (“Lost in the Middle”)
- The paper reports: “**performance can degrade significantly when changing the position of relevant information**” and models “**do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172 (Abstract)
- It also states performance is “**often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end** … and **significantly degrades** … in the **middle**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172 (Abstract)

This supports a key long-context limit: large windows don’t guarantee reliable retrieval/usage of all tokens.

---

### E) Length generalization beyond training & methods to extend (RoPE scaling / Position Interpolation)
- Position Interpolation paper: “**We present Position Interpolation (PI) that extends the context window sizes of RoPE-based … LLaMA … to up to 32768 with minimal fine-tuning** …”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15595 (Abstract)
- It motivates why naive extension can fail: extrapolating beyond trained length “**may lead to catastrophically high attention scores that completely ruin the self-attention mechanism**.”  
  Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15595 (Abstract)

So even with big windows, there’s a constraint: models may not generalize well to longer sequences unless you modify positional encoding handling and/or fine-tune.

---

### F) Practical usability limits: “more context isn’t automatically better” + context rot + need to curate/summarize
- Anthropic Claude docs: “**more context isn't automatically better. As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot. This makes curating what's in context just as important as how much space is available.**”  
  Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

This directly supports practical limitations such as:
- needing summarization/compaction,
- careful selection of what to include,
- and that long context can still degrade accuracy/recall.

---

## 3) Concise key takeaways (each tied to sources)

1) **Context windows have grown from ~1k tokens (GPT‑2) to 100k–200k (Claude) and even 1M (Gemini 1.5 Pro preview).**  
   - GPT‑2 1024 max positions: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/gpt2  
   - Claude 100k (May 2023): https://www.anthropic.com/news/100k-context-windows  
   - Claude 3 200k (Mar 2024): https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-family  
   - Gemini 1.5 Pro up to 1M (Feb 2024): https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/google-gemini-next-generation-model-february-2024/

2) **Scaling to long context remains expensive: transformer memory/compute grow quadratically with sequence length (for standard attention).**  
   Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172

3) **Inference memory becomes a hard bottleneck because KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and can dominate memory at long contexts.**  
   Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.18079

4) **Even if a model can accept long prompts, it may not use them reliably; accuracy often drops when relevant info is in the middle (“Lost in the Middle”).**  
   Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.03172

5) **Long-context capability often requires special techniques (e.g., Position Interpolation for RoPE) because naive length extrapolation can break attention behavior.**  
   Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15595

6) **Operationally, “more tokens” can cause “context rot”; practical systems must curate/summarize/compact context rather than blindly stuffing the window.**  
   Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

---

## Notable gaps / what I did NOT find (so you can act on it)

- **GPT‑3 explicit “2048 tokens context window” quote**: not successfully extracted from the GPT‑3 paper HTML with available tools. Source checked: https://arxiv.org/html/2005.14165
- **Primary-source OpenAI quotes for GPT‑4 32k and GPT‑4 Turbo 128k**: relevant OpenAI pages were blocked/unreadable when fetched (403/timeouts), so I only have search snippets for those pages:
  - GPT‑4 research page: https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-research/ (blocked to read)
  - DevDay GPT‑4 Turbo: https://openai.com/index/new-models-and-developer-products-announced-at-devday/ (blocked to read)
- **Direct O(n²) quote from Vaswani et al. 2017**: not found as a verbatim quote; instead cited quadratic scaling from “Lost in the Middle.”

args.content:
# Context windows in large language models: how they’ve changed and what limits remain

## What a “context window” is
A model’s context window is the maximum number of tokens it can condition on at once (input plus, in many APIs, the space reserved for output). Larger windows let models “see” more text, code, or conversation history in a single request, but they do **not** guarantee perfect recall or reasoning over all included content.

## How context windows have changed (selected milestones)

> Note: This timeline includes **only milestones that were supported by accessible, primary sources in the research findings**.

| Approx. date (per source) | Model / vendor | Context window (tokens) | Primary evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| (architecture doc) | GPT‑2 (via Transformers config) | 1,024 | GPT‑2 config: “`n_positions … defaults to 1024` — The maximum sequence length …” (Hugging Face) https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/gpt2 |
| Mar 2023 (model docs) | OpenAI GPT‑4 | 8,192 | OpenAI model docs list “8,192 context window” https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4 |
| Nov 2023+ (model docs) | OpenAI GPT‑4 Turbo | 128,000 | OpenAI model docs list “128,000 context window” https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4-turbo |
| May 2024+ (model docs) | OpenAI GPT‑4o | 128,000 | OpenAI model docs list “128,000 context window” https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4o |
| 2025 (model docs) | OpenAI GPT‑4.1 | ~1,000,000 | OpenAI model docs: “It features a 1M token context window” and “1,047,576 context window” https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1 |
| May 2023 | Anthropic Claude | 100,000 | “We’ve expanded Claude’s context window from 9K to 100K tokens” https://www.anthropic.com/news/100k-context-windows |

Practical implication: long-running assistants need explicit memory management (summaries, retrieval, or truncation policies) rather than assuming unlimited history.

### 6) Extending context length can require special techniques; naive extrapolation can fail
Research on extending RoPE-based models highlights failure modes when you push beyond trained lengths:
- Position Interpolation paper: extrapolating positional embeddings “may lead to **catastrophically high attention scores** that completely ruin… self-attention,” and presents a method to “extend… context window… to up to **32768** with minimal fine-tuning.” https://arxiv.org/html/2306.15595

Practical implication: “supports N tokens” is partly an engineering/training choice; pushing much longer may require dedicated training or positional-encoding adaptations.

## Conclusions
- Context windows have expanded dramatically—from ~1k tokens (GPT‑2 configuration) to **hundreds of thousands**, and in some product lines to **millions of tokens** (e.g., Google Gemini 1.5 Pro’s **2M** waitlist offering; OpenAI GPT‑4.1’s ~**1M** context in model docs; Anthropic docs listing **1M** for several Claude models).
- Even with huge windows, major limits remain: **compute/memory scaling**, **KV-cache memory pressure**, **latency/cost**, and **quality degradation** (including position-dependent failures and “context rot”).
- Operationally, large windows introduce system-design requirements: separate **output caps**, and explicit **overflow handling** (errors, truncation, summarization). In practice, you often still need careful context curation and memory strategies rather than simply “include everything.”
